subject: Computer / ICT
title: Types of Algorithms
sourceNote: Based on the provided lesson materials.

algorithms.name: Brute Force
algorithms.meaning: A simple, direct approach that tries all possible solutions systematically until a solution is found.
algorithms.example: Searching every possible combination for a solution, even when many choices are unnecessary.
algorithms.when: The problem is small enough that trying every possibility is practical, or when correctness is more important than speed.

algorithms.name: Recursive
algorithms.meaning: A problem-solving approach where a solution is expressed in terms of smaller instances of the same problem until a small base case is reached.
algorithms.example: The factorial function: n! = n × (n−1)! with a base case such as 1! = 1.
algorithms.when: A problem naturally repeats the same structure on smaller inputs.

algorithms.name: Divide and Conquer
algorithms.meaning: Divides a problem into smaller sub-problems, solves each part, and combines the results to solve the whole problem.
algorithms.example: Merge Sort divides a list into smaller lists, sorts them, then combines the sorted parts.
algorithms.when: A large problem can be separated into smaller, manageable sub-problems.

algorithms.name: Dynamic Programming
algorithms.meaning: Solves overlapping sub-problems while remembering previous results so the same calculations do not have to be repeated.
algorithms.example: A recursive calculation may repeatedly solve the same smaller problem; dynamic programming stores that result for later use.
algorithms.when: Sub-problems overlap and repeated calculations would waste time.

algorithms.name: Greedy
algorithms.meaning: Builds a solution step by step by choosing what appears to be the best option at the current moment without considering all future choices.
algorithms.example: At each step, choose the locally best available option in a problem where such choices can lead to a useful solution.
algorithms.when: Local choices can produce an appropriate or optimal solution for the problem.

algorithms.name: Randomized
algorithms.meaning: Uses random numbers or random choices to decide the next step or procedure.
algorithms.example: Randomized algorithms can choose a random pivot or random candidate to change which path is taken.
algorithms.when: Random choices can reduce predictable patterns or increase the chance of efficient behavior.

algorithms.name: Backtracking
algorithms.meaning: Searches possible choices and abandons a partial solution when it cannot lead to a feasible solution, then tries another choice.
algorithms.example: A maze solver follows a path and goes back when it reaches a dead end.
algorithms.when: A problem requires exploring combinations or paths while rejecting choices that cannot work.

keyTerms.definition: A sequence of steps used to solve a problem or perform a task.
The input or situation in which an algorithm takes minimum time.
The input or situation in which an algorithm takes maximum or long time.
An analysis based on typical or random inputs and their computation time.
Theoretical analysis performed before implementation, using assumptions about the computing environment.
Empirical analysis after implementation, using observed statistics such as time and space.
An optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems.
A recursive solution contains a small number of distinct sub-problems that are solved repeatedly.
A solution that satisfies the requirements or constraints of a problem.

guided.q: The algorithm tries every possible combination until it finds a solution.
guided.explanation: Brute force systematically explores possible solutions.

guided.q: The same type of problem is solved again with a smaller input until a base case is reached.
guided.explanation: Recursion solves smaller versions of the same problem.

guided.q: A large problem is divided into smaller parts, solved, and then combined.
guided.explanation: Divide and conquer follows divide → solve → combine.

guided.q: Previous answers are stored so repeated calculations can be avoided.
guided.explanation: Dynamic programming stores useful results from overlapping sub-problems.

guided.q: The algorithm chooses what seems best right now at each step.
guided.explanation: Greedy methods make locally best choices step by step.

guided.q: The next choice is influenced by a random number.
guided.explanation: Randomized algorithms use random choices in their procedure.

guided.q: A search follows a choice, but goes back when that choice cannot lead to a feasible solution.
guided.explanation: Backtracking explores choices and removes failed paths.

analysisCases.q: The input makes the algorithm finish in the minimum time.
The input makes the algorithm take the maximum amount of time.
analysisCases.explanation: Worst case represents maximum or long time.

analysisCases.q: Typical or random inputs are considered to estimate usual computation time.
You evaluate efficiency theoretically before the algorithm is implemented.
analysisCases.explanation: A priori analysis is theoretical and performed before implementation.

analysisCases.q: You run the implemented algorithm and collect time and space statistics.
analysisCases.explanation: Posterior analysis is empirical and performed after implementation.

scenarios.q: A maze program follows a path, then returns to the last decision point when it reaches a dead end.
scenarios.explanation: Returning from a failed path is the key idea of backtracking.

scenarios.q: A problem can be split into smaller independent pieces and the results can later be combined.
scenarios.explanation: Divide and conquer is built around splitting and combining.

scenarios.q: A problem has repeated sub-problems, so the program stores answers to reuse them.
scenarios.explanation: Dynamic programming avoids repeated work by remembering previous results.

think.q: Which clue most strongly suggests dynamic programming?
think.explanation: Dynamic programming is especially useful when sub-problems overlap and results can be reused.

think.q: Which clue most strongly suggests backtracking?
choices: Undo a choice when it cannot lead to a feasible solution
think.explanation: Backtracking explores a choice and reverses it when that path fails.

think.q: Which approach is most direct when the search space is small and every possibility can be checked?
think.explanation: Brute force systematically checks possibilities and is practical for small enough problems.

think.q: Which analysis asks what happens before implementation using theoretical measures?
think.explanation: A priori analysis is theoretical and occurs before implementation.

apply.q: Your team wants to sort data by splitting it into smaller lists, sorting them, then merging them.
apply.explanation: That is the divide → solve → combine pattern.

apply.q: A search program can save the result of a smaller calculation and reuse it later.
apply.explanation: Reusing stored sub-problem results is a core dynamic-programming idea.

apply.q: A decision process repeatedly chooses the best-looking option available at the current step.
apply.explanation: Greedy algorithms make local choices at each step.

quiz.q: Which algorithm systematically tries all possible solutions?
quiz.explanation: Brute force checks possible solutions systematically.

quiz.q: Which approach solves smaller versions of the same problem until a base case is reached?
quiz.explanation: Recursion uses smaller instances of the same problem.

quiz.q: Which algorithm divides a problem, solves the parts, and combines the results?
quiz.explanation: Divide and conquer follows the divide, solve, and combine pattern.

quiz.q: Which approach stores previous results to avoid repeating calculations?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic programming remembers useful results from sub-problems.

quiz.q: Which strategy makes a locally best choice at each step?
quiz.explanation: Greedy methods choose what appears best at the current step.

quiz.q: Which type uses random numbers or random choices in its procedure?
quiz.explanation: Randomized algorithms use randomness to influence choices.

quiz.q: Which strategy goes back after discovering that a choice cannot lead to a feasible solution?
quiz.explanation: Backtracking abandons failed partial solutions and tries another path.

quiz.q: Which case describes the minimum time taken by an algorithm?
quiz.explanation: Best case is the minimum-time situation.

quiz.q: Which analysis is theoretical and performed before implementation?
quiz.explanation: A priori analysis evaluates an algorithm theoretically before implementation.

quiz.q: Which statement is an advantage of algorithms noted in the lesson materials?
choices: They are easy to understand without programming knowledge.
They always use the fewest steps.
They can solve every possible problem.
quiz.explanation: The source notes that algorithms are easy to understand without programming knowledge. It also notes limitations such as processing time and difficulty handling some structures.

master.q: A school app has a small set of possible PIN combinations and can safely check each one. Which strategy is the most direct starting point?
master.explanation: When the search space is small enough, systematic checking is a direct brute-force approach.

master.q: A route problem is split into smaller parts, each part is solved, and the results are combined. Which strategy is this?
master.explanation: Divide and conquer divides, solves sub-problems, and combines results.

master.q: A calculation repeatedly encounters the same smaller sub-problems, so answers are stored for reuse. Which strategy?
master.explanation: Storing and reusing repeated sub-problem results is dynamic programming.

master.q: A maze solver tries a path and returns to the previous decision when the path becomes impossible. Which strategy?
master.explanation: Backtracking explores paths and reverses failed choices.

master.q: You want a theoretical efficiency estimate before the program is implemented. Which analysis?
master.explanation: A priori analysis is theoretical and done before implementation.

master.q: After implementation, you run the algorithm and record actual time and space behavior. Which analysis?
master.explanation: Posterior analysis uses observed statistics after implementation.
